observation.what_happens: A red ball on a string swings back and forth beneath a fixed support beside a striped scale. It is released from a small displacement to the right at about 4.0 s and continues swinging through the end of the clip.

calibration.note: black string = 0.6 m (narrator said thread length is sixty centimetres at 0.1 s) spans 313 ± 1.1 px in SAM's mask (read in 3 still frames)

pivot.why: the swing covers only 14° of arc; under 25° the path doesn't determine the radius (±2 px), so L isn't measured from it

given: scale: black string = 0.6 m (narrator said thread length is sixty centimetres at 0.1 s) spans 313 ± 1.1 px in SAM's mask (read in 3 still frames), known to ±2% (its size ±2%, its length in pixels ±0.34%)
thread length = 0.6 m (“धागे की लंबाई साठ सेंटीमीटर है।”)
reasoning: Theta is a ~0.12 rad sine with ~1.55 s period matching a 0.6 m pendulum and shows slight amplitude decay, so L is fixed at the stated 0.6 m and g sets the period. Candidates go from textbook undamped small-angle and sine laws to linear viscous and quadratic air-drag damping to test what best predicts the held-back decay.

critique.finding: The ball swings as a pendulum pulled by gravity with g = {g} and slowed by air with damping {gamma}. Its misses stay within the noise, so it captures the motion.
critique.headline: Air softly slows the swinging red ball.
critique.why_it_won: It includes gentle air friction that bleeds energy each swing, while the ideal pendulums without damping wander far outside the noise.

eyeball.confidence: medium for g from pendulum period, low for gamma from slow amplitude decay
eyeball.law_in_words: small-angle simple pendulum with viscous damping: angle'' + gamma*angle' + (g/L)*angle = 0 with L=0.6 m, period T ~ 2*pi*sqrt(L/g) and amplitude envelope ~ exp(-gamma*t/2)
